items.title: Trojanized 'Claude Code' extension 2.1.313 on Cursor's marketplace planted a persistent SSH backdoor
items.summary: A tampered build of the Claude Code extension (version 2.1.313) was served through Cursor's extension marketplace under the legitimate publisher name until removed on 30 Oct. Researchers say it added an attacker's SSH key and opened a reverse tunnel to an attacker-controlled server. Cursor says at most 5,000 users were affected and that the build was not developed by Anthropic. Ars Technica's headline puts the exposure at nearly 12 hours.
items.why_it_matters: AI coding-agent extensions run on machines holding credentials and repo access, making them a high-value supply-chain target. Uninstalling the extension reportedly does not remove the backdoor, so affected users must check for the key and rotate credentials.

learn.title: Report a kernel speedup honestly: ratio, latency cut and a bootstrap interval
learn.why_today: The story quotes 472 us against 518 us as a 9.8% gain, from a single livestream run.
learn.explanation: A speedup and a latency reduction are different numbers: 518/472 - 1 is about 9.7% faster, while 1 - 472/518 is about 8.9% less time. Quote which one you mean. A single timing also hides run-to-run noise from clocks, caches and scheduling, so repeat the measurement and bootstrap the ratio of mean latencies to get an interval. If the interval for 'B is faster than A' includes zero, the claim is not established. The snippet uses simulated, illustrative latencies centred on the reported figures; it is not ModelBest's data.
learn.math: s = \frac{\bar t_A}{\bar t_B} - 1,\quad c = 1 - \frac{\bar t_B}{\bar t_A}
learn.python:
import random, statistics as st
random.seed(0)
# Illustrative latencies in microseconds (NOT ModelBest's data): kernel A ~518 us, kernel B ~472 us
a = [random.gauss(518, 12) for _ in range(30)]
b = [random.gauss(472, 12) for _ in range(30)]
print("latency cut: %.1f%%" % (100 * (1 - st.mean(b) / st.mean(a))))
print("speedup (a/b - 1): %.1f%%" % (100 * (st.mean(a) / st.mean(b) - 1)))
def boot():
    ra = [random.choice(a) for _ in a]; rb = [random.choice(b) for _ in b]
    return st.mean(ra) / st.mean(rb) - 1
xs = sorted(boot() for _ in range(2000))
print("95%% CI speedup: %.1f%% .. %.1f%%" % (100 * xs[50], 100 * xs[1949]))

learn.title: Write causal softmax attention from scratch, and check a one-line invariant
learn.why_today: The reported kernel targets a prefill attention path, the computation below in its plainest form.
learn.explanation: Attention for query i is a softmax over scaled dot products with keys 0..i, then a weighted sum of values. Subtracting the row maximum before exponentiating keeps exp from overflowing without changing the result. Causality means the first token can only attend to itself, so its output must equal V[0] exactly, a cheap invariant to test any optimised kernel against a slow reference. Real kernels fuse these steps and tile them through on-chip memory; the maths is unchanged. Sizes here are illustrative.
learn.python:
import math, random
random.seed(1)
T, d = 4, 8
Q = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(d)] for _ in range(T)]
K = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(d)] for _ in range(T)]
V = [[random.gauss(0, 1) for _ in range(d)] for _ in range(T)]
def attn(Q, K, V):
    out = []
    for i, q in enumerate(Q):
        s = [sum(x * y for x, y in zip(q, K[j])) / math.sqrt(d) for j in range(i + 1)]  # causal
        m = max(s); e = [math.exp(x - m) for x in s]; z = sum(e)
        out.append([sum(e[j] / z * V[j][c] for j in range(i + 1)) for c in range(d)])
    return out
o = attn(Q, K, V)
print("row0 equals V[0]:", all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(o[0], V[0])))
print("out[3][:3] =", [round(x, 3) for x in o[3][:3]])
